steps.title: Light and crisp
steps.body: Melon de Bourgogne, often just Melon, gives light, very dry whites with lemon, green apple, pear, white flowers and a saline, mineral note. Acidity is high, alcohol moderate, often 12% or less; Muscadet is legally capped at 12% for most wines. It's neutral in aroma, which makes lees ageing important.

steps.title: From Burgundy to the sea
steps.body: As its name says, Melon came from Burgundy. It's a cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc, a sibling of Chardonnay. After the harsh winter of 1709 killed many vines near Nantes, growers replanted with frost-resistant Melon. It became the grape of Muscadet, near the Loire's mouth. Burgundy later banned it.

steps.prompt: Why was Melon planted near Nantes?
options: It survived the harsh winter of 1709
steps.explanation: After the 1709 freeze, frost-resistant Melon replaced lost vines.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for very pale colour, a subtle nose of lemon, apple and sea air, and a light, crisp, saline palate. Lees-aged versions add bread and a slight creaminess, and sometimes a tiny spritz. Compared with Pinot Grigio, it's more saline and mineral.

steps.prompt: Melon de Bourgogne is a sibling of Chardonnay.
steps.explanation: Yes. Both are crosses of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Melon gives light, crisp, saline whites
It came from Burgundy and replaced vines near Nantes after 1709
